What you need to know
- El Nino-driven heat could cause nearly 16,000 deaths in India by February, a new Climate Impact Lab report says
- Electoral roll revision causes rift within Election Commission of India: report
- Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi to visit Canada in December, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says
- ECI defends internal disagreements, says 'normal part' of deliberations
- Asian Games: India grabs four more medals in shooting, weight lifting and tennis

SC refers matter of Election Commission appointments to larger bench
A two-judge bench of the Supreme Court of India on Wednesday heard petitions challenging a controversial 2023 law which changed the appointment process for the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners.
The new law formed an appointing committee comprised the prime minister, leader of opposition and a union cabinet minister, nominated by the prime minister instead of the Chief Justice of India, as prescribed by the Supreme Court.
Critics questioned the inclusion of the cabinet minister instead of an independent chief justice and argued that such a process would impede the independence of the election authority in India.
On Wednesday, a two-judge bench of the apex court disagreed on how to proceed, ultimately referring the matter to a three-judge bench.
Justice Dipankar Datta opined that the new appointment method failed the "perception trust," as reported by legal media outlet Live Law.
"Free and fair elections depend on a truly independent ECI. It is not enough for the ECI to be independent; it must appear to be independent. The member nominated by the prime minister cannot be expected to defy the prime minister," Justice Datta observed, speaking of the cabinet minister.
Meanwhile, Justice Satish Chandra Sharma observed that the issue would have to be determined by a Constitutional Bench since it involved substantial Interpretation of the Indian constitution.
Rahul Gandhi accuses ECI of 'vote theft' after report of internal rift
Rahul Gandhi, a key opposition leader of India and one of the most outspoken critics of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, accused the Election Commission of India (ECI) of "treason" on Wednesday after the Indian Express report on internal rifts regarding the countrywide revision of electoral rolls.
"Vote chori is a crime against the Indian people and a direct attack on our constitution," he said in a post on X, insinuating that the commission had acted on the behest of Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and its ideological parent, Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS).
The RSS is a right-wing group that has produced several leaders in the current Indian government and positions itself as the guardian of Hindu values in India.
"The time will come when we catch hold of you. You won't be spared," Gandhi said in a video message in Hindi.
This is not the first time India's opposition, or even Gandhi, has accused the ECI of bending rules to favor the Modi government. In 2025, Gandhi had accused the government of 'vote theft' in the 2024 national elections. He had alleged that electoral rolls in a key state had been manipulated to favor Prime Minister Modi's BJP.
More recently, he has accused Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of favoring the BJP government when he is supposed to remain unbiased.
WATCH: Can Startups turn India into a global space power?
India's private space sector has reached a major milestone. Skyroot Aerospace has become the first Indian private company to place an independently developed rocket into orbit, marking a breakthrough for India's fast-growing commercial space industry.
The successful launch of Vikram-1 underscores how government reforms, rising investment and a new generation of engineers are reshaping the country’s ambitions in the global space race.
From Hyderabad's thriving startup ecosystem to universities training future aerospace talent, momentum is building around satellite launches, space technology and private innovation.
As India looks to expand its share of the global space economy, companies such as Skyroot are testing whether the country can not only develop advanced rockets, but also compete with established space powers in an increasingly strategic and lucrative market.
ECI defends internal disagreements, says 'normal part' of deliberations
The Election Commission of India on Wednesday asserted that all directions issued by the body carried "full legal sanctions" and that disagreements within the commission were a "normal part" of deliberations in any institute.
Its statement, posted in a press note on social media, came in response to an Indian Express report which said two of the three commissioners of the ECI had repeatedly made formal objections to several aspects of the nationwide revision of voter rolls in India (see entry below)
The story pointed to an unprecedented rift within the institute, which is integral to maintaining the integrity of elections in the world's largest democracy.
"Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institute," the ECI said in the press note.
"Highlighting certain specific internal notes/observations spread over the period of 10 months while overlooking the much larger body of approvals, decisions, instructions and initiatives give only one part of the picture," it said.
The statement said the ECI had taken around 40 new initiatives and undertaken several electoral reforms in recent months, including the conduct of electoral roll revision across the country.
"All these decisions are an outcome of the unanimous decisions of the full Commission in the past one year," it said.
Delhi Women's college rolls back decision to move classes online after suspected rape of minor
Lady Shri Ram College for Women (LSR), a leading institute in New Delhi, said it would resume classes offline starting Thursday, soon after it shifted classes online over the alleged rape of a minor girl in a nearby neighborhood.
"Meetings are going on offline with a large number of students and faculty. Offline classes and regular schedule shall resume from tomorrow," said LSR principal Kanika K Ahuja said, according to the Press Trust of India.
The college had shifted Wednesday's classes online citing concerns over its students' safety in the light of an alleged gang-rape. On Monday evening, a 17-year-old was allegedly raped by three men in a south Delhi locality, less than 10 minutes away from LSR, while her male friend was held down.
Authorities have reportedly arrested all three suspects, and a formal investigation is underway.
Opposition leaders and critics have questioned the state of law and order in the national capital and the message that LSR's former decision sends to the city's population.
Electoral roll revision causes rift within Election Commission of India: report
Two out of three of India's election commissioners have raised several issues regarding India's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls, time and time again on record, the Indian Express reported on Wednesday. This marks an unprecedented rift within the institute widely considered integral to maintaining India's democratic integrity.
Election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi both formally objected on record, at least 14 times in the last 10 months, to decisions taken and orders issued against their knowledge, the paper reported. Four of those complaints were made in a single day.
These objections dealt with new voter registrations, deletion and restoration of voters in the rolls, filing of appeals against orders restoring voters in the SIR process and the custody and security of the entire electoral roll itself, the report said.
In one of the objections, Sandhu complained that the Election Commission acted against the written advice of two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."
Why does this matter?
Sandhu and Joshi, along with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, are responsible for overseeing the SIR exercise. The process is meant to remove redundancies in India's electoral rolls.
Opposition leaders and critics have argued that those struck off in the exercise include a heavy proportion of minority voters and that Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP is using it as a tool to secure future electoral wins. They have also accused ECI chief Kumar of doing the central government's bidding even though the institute is meant to maintain its independence.
The BJP has dismissed such claims, arguing that those removed largely involve dead voters and illegal infiltrators, thereby protecting India's democracy.
Over 130 million Indian voters have been struck off the draft voters list across 30 states and union territories, the report said, putting the ECI in the middle of a national debate over who votes and who doesn't.
Asian Games: India grabs four more medals in shooting, weight lifting and tennis
Indian athletes won four more medals in the ongoing Asian Games in Japan on Wednesday, taking the nation's tally to 11 so far.
Mirabai Chanu, an athlete from the northeastern state of Manipur, clinched a silver medal in the 49-kilogram category after lifting a total of 198 kilograms. She became the second Indian, after Karnam Malleswari, to win medals at all major international weightlifting events, as per India's Department of Sports.
India also won two bronze medals after the men's and women's skeet teams reached yet another podium for shooting.
The latest win came from Jay Meena, who won a bronze in men's singles soft tennis. Meena's victory scripted history, marking India's first medal in the sport.
This brings India's tally to one gold, five silvers and five bronze medals on day five.
PM Modi expected to visit Canada around December: Mark Carney
Prime Minister Narendra Modi is set to visit Canada in December 2026, around the G20 meet in United States, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters in New York on Tuesday.
Carney's remark was in response to a question about Modi's pending visit and how close Ottawa was to concluding a free trade agreement with Delhi.
"We are making good progress in our trade negotiations with India. It is an exceptionally important relationship on many, many levels, people-to-people levels, security levels, and also trade and economic," he said, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Carney said Modi had, at last year's G20 meet, committed to concluding a trade deal with Canada within the year.
"I believe that India just confirmed that the prime minister will be visiting Canada around that time. The precise date isn't out, but I very much look forward to hosting him," the Canadian leader said after pointing out that Modi would already be in the US for G20 in December.
New Delhi has not yet publicly confirmed the trip.
Modi last visited Canada to attend the G7 summit in June 2025.
New Delhi and Ottawa have been rebuilding frayed diplomatic ties since Carney took over from former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau. In 2023, India-Canada relations hit the pit over sharp disagreements onSikh separatism, resulting in the expulsion of diplomats and escalating claims.
With Modi's 2025 trip to Canada, both countries began repairing ties, this time focusing on trade. And both countries have at least one mammoth reason to — diversifying away from their reliance on a volatile United States.
El Nino-driven heat could kill thousands in India by February: report
This year's powerful El Nino phenomenon, which is driving global heat to record levels and contributing to severe droughts, wildfires and water shortages, is likely to cause 15,800 deaths in India by the end of February, according to a research report released on Wednesday.
The warning, released by the University of Chicago-based Climate Impact Lab, said as many as 451,000 more deaths between June and February of next year could be attributed to El Nino, when compared to typical heat-related deaths in a year.
El Nino is a natural climate phenomenon that occurs every two to seven years, toward the end of the year. It comes in various strengths — depending on the prevailing conditions.
El Nino patterns are considered strong if the surface temperature of the water off the west coast of South America is over 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above average. In July this year, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) was already observing temperature increases ofgreater than 3 degrees Celsius in the eastern and central Pacific.
The Climate Impact Lab report said the powerful heat this year was most dangerous in places that are already hot and relatively poor. It projected that the Global South will see more heat-related deaths.
What could help prevent deaths?
Heat warnings, hydration outreach, cooling centers and a plan to cope with the heat are all ways governments can help protect people, the report said, adding that they should also expand hospital capacity and chalk out anticipatory financing.
Abhiyant Tiwari, a heat expert at NRDC India who was not involved in the study, said the report's projections should serve as a call to action rather than be another reason for alarm.
But while it's one thing to have well thought-out plans — as India does — implementing these plans remains a challenge, he said.
"The real measure of our preparedness is not how many heat warnings we issue, but how effectively we protect people and reduce preventable deaths," Tiwari said.
Welcome to our coverage!
Hello! and welcome to DW's India new blog.
This is Mahima Kapoor reporting from the national capital, where the mood is somber, even often angry, over the recent incidents of alleged rape against minors and women.
A minor was reportedly gang-raped near a temple in southeast Delhi on Monday evening and the authorities have arrested at least one of the three accused. Today, a renowned women's college in the vicinity said it would switch to online classes to keep students safe.
Continuing on the somber front, a new report by the Climate Impact Lab said that El Nino-driven heat could kill over 450,000 people across the world by the end of February and that nearly 16,000 of those are projected to be from India.
Meanwhile, a controversy is brewing in the Election Commission of India. A report by the Indian Express said two of the three members of the Election Commission have, several times now, raised questions internally about the controversial revision of electoral rolls across India that struck 13 crore voter names from the list so far.
On the international front, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney revealed that New Delhi has confirmed a visit from Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in December.
And India's foreign minister is currently in New York for the United Nations General Assembly, advocating for the Global South.
Stay tuned for all of this and more.
